en: The Pasig River flows westward into Manila Bay because its source, Laguna de Bay, sits at a higher elevation than the sea.
The Habagat monsoon brings heavy rain to western Luzon because ocean winds from the West Philippine Sea drop moisture upon hitting the Zambales Mountains.
Coron’s dramatic limestone cliffs formed over millions of years as acidic rainwater slowly dissolved ancient coral reefs uplifted by tectonic forces.
The Chico River transports nutrient-rich silt from the Cordillera mountains to the Cagayan Valley, naturally fertilizing downstream agricultural plains during the wet season.
Laguna de Bay formed when tectonic shifts and volcanic activity blocked the natural drainage of surrounding lowlands, creating a massive lake basin.
Tubbataha Reef thrives because strong Sulu Sea ocean currents continuously sweep nutrient-rich waters across the atoll, feeding its diverse and vibrant coral polyps.
The Sierra Madre mountain range protects eastern Luzon from severe typhoons because its dense, towering forests absorb strong winds and trap heavy rainfall.
Mayon Volcano’s frequent eruptions deposit thick layers of volcanic ash that weather into highly fertile soil, creating ideal conditions for growing Bicol's famous abaca plants.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River formed when slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolved the underlying limestone bedrock, carving out a massive underground cave system.
Strong tidal currents in the San Bernardino Strait mix deep, nutrient-rich waters with surface waters, supporting a highly productive and diverse marine ecosystem.
Underground magma beneath Mount Malinao heats groundwater into steam, which geothermal plants in Albay capture through wells to generate clean, renewable electricity.
Maria Cristina Falls generates hydroelectric power because the Agus River drops sharply from Lake Lanao's high elevation, creating strong water pressure to spin turbines.
